name: Label sheet
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/label-sheet/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: Labels that come off a printer and get stuck onto things: a bin label on a rack, a batch label on a drum, a pallet tag, a QC hold sticker. Either a grid of them on an A4 sheet of die-cut stock or one at a time on a continuous roll, sized in millimetres because the stock in the printer is.
when_to_use: The output is adhesive stock a machine will scan and a person will stick onto something — a rack beam, a drum, a pallet, an incoming carton. The line against document-page is the medium and it is not a matter of degree: a document is A4 paperwork a person reads, signs and files, sized so a clerk can read a tax figure, and its failure is a wrong number; a label is stock a scanner reads, sized to the die-cut in the printer, and its failure is a symbol that will not scan or a sheet that peels two millimetres out of register across a whole shipment. Reach for document-page whenever the artefact carries terms, totals or a signature. Reach for focus-page for the other half of this workflow — the shop-floor screen that scans these labels back in at the gate or the rack, which is a task on a screen and prints nothing. Reach for card when the thing is a bordered panel grouping one region of a screen: a card is furniture measured in rem that reflows with the viewport, and a label is a physical object measured in millimetres that must not reflow at all. The test is whether a millimetre matters. If it does, it is this.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in page, and the shell is chrome. The toolbar, the stock selector, the offset controls and the page heading all carry print:hidden; what is left is the stock. app-shell's own rail and topbar do not carry print:hidden today, which document-page already flagged — a sheet printed from inside the shell as it stands comes out with the navigation down the left of it, and on label stock that lands the navigation across the first column of labels. Closing it is a decision for a person, in app-shell.

The print rules are document-page's and this entry does not restate them: chrome carries print:hidden, backgrounds do not print so nothing may carry meaning in a fill, break-inside-avoid on anything that must not split, and @page is hand-written CSS rather than a utility. Three things a label needs that a sheet of A4 does not are extensions of those, not replacements — the size is exact rather than capped, there is no secondary text colour, and the printer has to be told not to scale.

Every dimension a label has is exact and written in millimetres. 63.5 × 38.1 mm across a 210 mm sheet with a 7.25 mm side margin, a 2.5 mm column gutter and a 15.15 mm top margin is not a layout choice, it is the die-cut in the stock, and the three numbers have to add back to 210.0 or every label in the third column runs off its backing. What may flex is what is inside the label: the type wraps, the description clamps, and a long item name loses its tail. What may not flex is the box. A label sized in rem, in percentages, or as a fraction of its container is a label that is correct on the screen it was designed on and wrong on the stock.

There is no secondary text colour on a label. document-page stops at zinc-600 because zinc-500 is grey mush through an office laser; a thermal printer is worse than an office laser — it is one bit deep, so it has no grey at all and dithers zinc-600 into a checkerboard that at 11px reads as a smudge. Everything printed on a label is zinc-900 and the hierarchy is size and weight. zinc-600 survives in this entry only in the screen chrome, which never reaches the stock.

The label box takes overflow-hidden, which is the class document-page rules out on a document, and the reason the two disagree is the reason for the rule rather than an exception to it. There, overflow other than visible makes an element monolithic in paged media and a long line table is clipped at the first page break instead of splitting across it. Here monolithic is exactly what is wanted: a label that splits across two pages is two half labels on two pieces of stock. The scroller that holds the sheet on screen is the one place the old trap still bites, so it is cancelled with print:overflow-visible — a job of four sheets inside a live scroller prints the first one and stops.

The barcode is not drawn. A scannable Code 128 or QR symbol needs a font or a library and this stack has neither, and a barcode invented out of divs is worse than no barcode: it looks right in a review, it reaches the printer, and it fails at the gate at six in the morning with a lorry behind it. Every variant reserves the symbol's area at its exact printed size, with a border that survives onto the paper, and puts the human-readable value under it in the position a real label puts it. A sheet that comes out with empty ruled boxes on it is obviously wrong and gets caught in the first print; a sheet with a blank gap where a symbol should be looks fine. Whether the library takes a barcode dependency, and in which layer, is a decision for a person.

The human-readable line under the symbol is not a caption, it is the fallback, and it is what somebody keys in when the scanner will not read a scuffed label. So it is never truncated, never smaller than the label's own body size, and it carries the whole identifier. Descriptions truncate; codes do not. That is document-page's rule about identifiers, applied to the one line on the label most likely to be typed by hand.

Alignment is a workflow and not a setting. No printer agrees with anybody's stock on the first try, and the drift is a millimetre or two of feed rather than anything the operator did wrong, so the align variant is a real screen: a registration pattern printed onto the stock, an offset in millimetres in each axis, and a statement of what the operator does with the result. The offset applies on screen as well as on paper, because a preview that does not carry the correction is a preview of a different sheet.

The offset moves the grid with a margin rather than a transform. A transformed element is monolithic in paged media for the same reason an overflowing one is, so a translated grid takes its whole sheet with it and a two-sheet job breaks at the first page. A negative top margin is the one mechanism that shifts a block in both directions without fragmenting it.

The registration marks are drawn with type. A corner mark has to be black to be lined up against a die-cut edge, and the border tokens stop at border-zinc-300, which is about 16% grey and dithers on a thermal printer into something that cannot be registered against anything. document-page hit the same wall and took weight instead of inventing a darker token; this entry takes a plus sign, because a glyph is ink at full strength and needs no token at all. The label outlines beside them stay border-zinc-300 and are the secondary aid, not the mark.

Sheet stock gets part-used. Eight labels come off a sheet on Tuesday and the same sheet goes back in the drawer, so the print on Friday starts at position nine. The skipped positions are rendered as real empty cells and never dropped from the grid — remove them and every label after them moves up one position, which is the whole defect the start position exists to prevent. On screen they carry a bg-zinc-50 fill and their position number so the operator can check the count against the sheet in their hand; on paper they are simply blank, which says the same thing, because the sticker is already gone.

The print dialog has to be told not to help. Scale must be 100% and Fit to page must be off, or a 63.5 mm label comes out at 60.4 mm and no offset will fix it; margins must be None, because the stock's own margins are already in the markup and the dialog will add its own on top. Background graphics stays off, which is why nothing here depends on a fill. None of that is settable from the page and all of it is on the screen next to the Print button, because it is the difference between one wasted sheet and a box of them.

The outer four millimetres or so of a laser page are physically unprintable whatever the margin says. Die-cut stock leaves 7.25 mm at the sides and 15.15 mm top and bottom for exactly that reason, so the labels are safely inside it — but a label design that runs ink to its own edge loses it on the outer column, and a full-bleed label is a thing this stack cannot produce.

There is no h1 on a label. document-page puts the h1 on the paper because a purchase order has a title block; a 38 mm label has room for a location and a symbol and nothing else, so the h1 names what is about to be printed, sits above the stock, and carries print:hidden with the rest of the chrome. It is still exactly one per page.

The values are the server's. Nothing on a label is computed in the browser — not the quantity, not the expiry, not the check digit that a real symbol carries. The Alpine on these variants is in the chrome: the start position, the offset, the quantity, and the count of what will come out.

anatomy.description: The zinc-100 page the stock sits on, so the preview reads as stock on a desk. print:bg-white print:p-0 — on paper there is no desk.
The h1, the count and what stock it is going onto. print:hidden, and it is the only heading on the page.
Stock, quantity, start position, Print and Download PDF, with the dialog settings stated beside them. Sticky on screen, print:hidden, and the only part of the page carrying state.

The sheet at its real size — w-[210mm] with the stock's own px-[7.25mm] py-[15.15mm] — inside an overflow-x-auto print:overflow-visible box. The box is the whole 390px answer: physical size does not reflow, so it scrolls instead.
grid-cols-3 gap-x-[2.5mm] gap-y-0 inside the stock margins, which resolves each column to exactly 63.5 mm. The gutter is the die-cut, not a design gap.
One die-cut position: a fixed h-[38.1mm] box with overflow-hidden and break-inside-avoid, bordered on screen and print:border-0 on paper, where the border is the physical cut.
A reserved box at the symbol's exact printed size with a ruled edge that prints. The substitution point, and the only thing on the label that is not real.
The identifier under the symbol, at label body size, never truncated. What gets keyed in when the scan fails.
A part-used sheet's already-peeled cells: empty, aria-hidden, holding their place in the grid, bg-zinc-50 on screen and blank on paper.

Four plus signs near the corners of every position, drawn in type rather than in rules because a mark that is 16% grey cannot be registered against anything. The offset that produced the sheet is printed with it, absolutely positioned into the stock's bottom margin so it displaces nothing.
Across and down in millimetres, stepped in halves, applied as a margin on the grid so the printed sheet and the preview move together.
Scale 100%, Fit to page off, margins None. Not settable from the page, so it is stated beside the button that opens the dialog.

behaviour: Nothing on a label moves. It has no hover, no disclosure and no tooltip; it is going onto a drum. Everything that moves is in the chrome above the stock.

Print calls window.print() on the sheet already on screen. It does not re-render into a hidden frame — the sheet the operator checked against the stock in their hand is the sheet that has to reach the printer.
Changing the start position redraws the grid with that many empty cells at the front and pushes the same labels down. The count strip and the sheet cannot disagree, because both read the same number.

Changing the quantity changes the number of sheets, and the count says so before the job goes: a hundred labels at a start of nine is five sheets, not four, and the difference is found either here or in the drawer.

The offset applies to the grid on screen and on paper at the same moment. Half a millimetre a press, capped at three, which is as far as the 7.25 mm side margin will absorb before the outer column of labels lands inside the unprintable edge of the page.

The alignment print is one sheet of registration marks and it is meant to be thrown away. The operator holds it against the die-cut stock, reads which way and how far it is out, enters that, and prints one more.

At 390px the stock does not reflow. The sheet keeps its 210 mm and scrolls sideways inside its own box, which is the same exception document-page takes for a line table and taken for the same reason: a preview that rearranged itself to fit a phone is a preview of something that will never come out of the printer. The phone variant is the arrangement that does work in a hand — one label, one printer, one button, and no sheet at all.

A record with no code prints its label with the human-readable line and the symbol area left empty and marked. A symbol generated from an empty string is a valid symbol that scans as nothing, and that failure surfaces at a gate rather than at a desk.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 is in the print head above the stock rather than on a label. Regions below it are h2, and on the stock itself there are no headings at all — a label is a record, not a document with an outline.

The sheet is an <ol role="list"> and each position an <li>, so the count and the position are announced. The role is written out because WebKit drops the list role from a list whose list-style is none, and preflight sets that on every ol before anybody writes a class.

Skipped positions are aria-hidden and empty. They exist to hold their place in the grid, and a screen reader that announced eight blank list items before the first real label would be reading the stock rather than the job.
The symbol area is aria-hidden. What it will hold is a picture of the value already written underneath it in text, and the reserved box says nothing to anybody until it is substituted.
The identifier under the symbol is text at full size in the reading order. It is the fallback for a scanner and for a reader alike, and it is the one thing on the label that is never truncated.

The count strip is role="status" so a change of quantity or start position is announced. It is the only live region on the page and it carries one sentence — how many labels, how many sheets, where they start.

The offset fields are real number inputs with the unit in the label rather than in a suffix, so the field is announced as "Across, millimetres" and not as a number with a symbol beside it. Both wear the wrapper focus outline every field in this system wears.
Print is a <button> and Download PDF is an <a> to a server route, named for what they do — Print 21 bin labels, Download as PDF. Print changes nothing and goes nowhere, so it is not a link.
Nothing on the page is autofocused. A stray Enter left over from the previous screen must not be able to start a print job.
